title: Wall Street Steadies as Oil Slips Below $100 Ahead of Big Fed Week
summary: US stocks stabilised on Friday as Brent crude fell below $100 a barrel, easing inflation worries, with investors bracing for a packed week of Federal Reserve policy, second-quarter GDP and inflation data, and megacap tech earnings.
description: US equities looked set to steady on Friday after a bruising session, as a retreat in oil prices helped calm inflation nerves at the end of a jittery week. Brent crude slipped below $100 a barrel, clawing back some of the ground lost earlier when renewed inflation fears and anxiety over heavy artificial intelligence spending knocked shares lower. The tech-heavy Nasdaq had tumbled more than 2% on Thursday, its worst single day in over a month, as investors questioned whether the enormous capital outlays behind the AI boom will pay off. Attention now turns to a dense calendar in the week ahead. The Federal Reserve's policy meeting concludes on Wednesday, with second-quarter gross domestic product and the personal consumption expenditures price index, the Fed's preferred inflation gauge, due the following day. Earnings from heavyweights including Microsoft, Meta and Apple are also on deck. With the S&P 500 hovering near record territory, traders are weighing whether resilient growth and cooling energy costs can offset sticky inflation and stretched valuations across the largest technology names heading into the second half of the year.
image_alt: Stock market trading screens representing US equities (illustrative)
key_points: Brent crude slipped below $100 a barrel, easing inflation concerns.
The Nasdaq fell more than 2% on Thursday amid AI-spending jitters, its worst day in over a month.
The Federal Reserve's policy meeting concludes Wednesday, with Q2 GDP and PCE data due Thursday.
Earnings from Microsoft, Meta and Apple are due in the week ahead.
why_it_matters: The Fed decision, inflation data and megacap earnings could set the tone for markets and borrowing costs into the second half, affecting retirement accounts and investor confidence.

title: Bank of Korea Raises Rates to 2.75% in First Hike in Over Three Years
summary: The Bank of Korea lifted its benchmark rate by a quarter point to 2.75%, its first increase since early 2023, as a semiconductor-led growth surge and housing and inflation risks tilted the central bank toward tightening.
description: The Bank of Korea raised its base rate by 25 basis points to 2.75%, its first interest-rate increase in more than three years, marking a decisive turn away from the easing cycle that had cut borrowing costs by a full percentage point since late 2024. Policymakers said economic growth was strengthening, led by exports and investment, while inflation was expected to stay above target for a considerable period and financial-stability risks persisted. The move followed a record run for the country's exports, which surged about 71% year-on-year in June on booming demand for semiconductors and AI-related components, the fastest pace since 1978. Governor Shin Hyun-song signalled the bank's existing 2.6% growth forecast for 2026 now looked too low and could be revised substantially higher in August. The central bank projected headline inflation of about 2.7% for the year and flagged uncertainty around the won, wage pressures and the pace of domestic demand recovery. Analysts said that with inflation likely to remain elevated and growth robust, further tightening is probable, noting the economy appears well placed to absorb higher rates.
image_alt: Korean won banknotes representing central bank policy (illustrative)
key_points: The Bank of Korea raised its base rate to 2.75%, its first hike since early 2023.
Exports surged about 71% year-on-year in June on semiconductor demand.
The bank projected 2026 headline inflation of about 2.7% and flagged upside risks.
Officials signalled the 2.6% growth forecast may be revised sharply higher in August.
why_it_matters: A shift to rate hikes raises borrowing costs for South Korean households and businesses and signals confidence that the chip-driven boom can withstand tighter policy.

title: ECB Holds Key Interest Rates Steady as It Watches Energy Shock
summary: The European Central Bank kept its three key interest rates unchanged, saying it is closely monitoring the inflationary impact of the Middle East energy shock while remaining committed to returning inflation to its 2% target.
description: The European Central Bank left its three key interest rates unchanged following its July meeting in Frankfurt, opting to hold as it assesses the inflationary fallout from higher energy prices tied to the conflict in the Middle East. The Governing Council said the outlook for energy prices, while highly volatile, currently stood close to the baseline of its June staff projections but well above pre-conflict levels, and warned that the full inflationary impact of the shock had yet to play out. Policymakers said they were closely watching the intensity and duration of the energy shock along with its indirect and second-round effects on prices, and reaffirmed a commitment to setting policy so that inflation stabilises at the 2% target over the medium term. The decision keeps the deposit rate steady after a period of adjustment and reflects a cautious, data-dependent stance amid elevated uncertainty. Euro-area growth has been subdued, weighed down by high energy costs, though officials expect activity to strengthen in the second half of the year if energy prices ease as anticipated. President Christine Lagarde stressed the council remains ready to act as the outlook evolves.
image_alt: Euro currency symbol representing European Central Bank policy (illustrative)
key_points: The ECB kept its three key interest rates unchanged at its July meeting.
It said the full inflationary impact of the Middle East energy shock has yet to play out.
The council is closely monitoring the shock's intensity, duration and second-round effects.
The ECB reaffirmed its commitment to returning inflation to the 2% target.
why_it_matters: ECB rate decisions shape borrowing costs across the euro area, so a hold amid an energy-driven inflation threat affects mortgages, business lending and growth in Europe's largest economies.

title: Bank of England Warns Cyber Risk Now Top Threat to UK Financial System
summary: The Bank of England's July Financial Stability Report flags intensifying cyber risk, with 82% of surveyed firms citing cyberattacks as a top-five systemic threat, while keeping the countercyclical capital buffer at 2%.
description: The Bank of England used its July Financial Stability Report to warn that cyber risk has intensified and now ranks as one of the most pressing threats to the UK financial system. The bank's 2026 first-half Systemic Risk Survey found that 82% of banks, insurers and asset managers cited cyberattacks as a top-five risk, underscoring how heavily critical financial services depend on complex digital infrastructure and shared third-party technology. Officials cautioned that rapidly advancing frontier AI models could accelerate the discovery and exploitation of vulnerabilities, creating potential system-wide consequences through correlated exposures at common suppliers. The report reinforced the importance of a joint statement issued in May by the Bank, the Financial Conduct Authority and HM Treasury on frontier models, and pointed to the newly launched oversight of Critical Third Parties, which began in mid-July. The Financial Policy Committee kept the countercyclical capital buffer at 2%, noting that global risks had risen amid geopolitical tensions, trade fragmentation and sovereign-debt pressures, even as domestic indicators stayed near long-run averages. It also recommended reviewing the loan-to-income limit on mortgage lending to ensure lenders can use it more fully.
image_alt: Cybersecurity systems representing financial-system cyber risk (illustrative)
key_points: 82% of surveyed UK firms cited cyberattacks as a top-five systemic risk.
The Bank warned advancing AI models could speed up exploitation of vulnerabilities.
The countercyclical capital buffer was held at 2% amid rising global risks.
Oversight of Critical Third Parties began in mid-July 2026.
why_it_matters: Cyber threats to banks and insurers can disrupt payments and services for millions, so regulators' focus on resilience shapes how safely the financial system operates.

title: Prudential-HCL Venture Becomes India's Eighth Standalone Health Insurer
summary: India's insurance regulator has registered a Prudential-HCL Group joint venture as the country's eighth standalone health insurer, its third new insurance registration of 2026, signalling continued expansion in the fast-growing health segment.
description: India's insurance regulator has granted a registration to a joint venture between UK-based Prudential and the HCL Group, making it the country's eighth standalone health insurer. The approval marks the Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India's third insurance registration of calendar year 2026, reflecting sustained interest in one of the world's fastest-growing insurance markets. Standalone health insurers focus exclusively on health cover, distinct from general insurers that also write motor, property and other lines, and the segment has expanded rapidly as rising incomes, medical inflation and greater awareness drive demand for protection. The new entrant is expected to intensify competition in retail health insurance, potentially spurring product innovation, wider distribution and sharper pricing for consumers. The registration aligns with the regulator's broader push to widen access under its 'Insurance for All by 2047' vision, supported by reforms that have eased foreign ownership rules and streamlined approvals to attract fresh capital and new players. Health insurance has been a key driver of the industry's growth, though it has also generated a significant share of customer complaints, making the arrival of well-capitalised entrants with global expertise a notable development for the market's next phase.
image_alt: Stethoscope and health insurance documents representing a new health insurer (illustrative)
key_points: A Prudential-HCL Group venture became India's eighth standalone health insurer.
It is IRDAI's third new insurance registration of 2026.
The move intensifies competition in the fast-growing retail health segment.
It aligns with the 'Insurance for All by 2047' access goals and eased foreign ownership rules.
why_it_matters: More health insurers can mean greater choice, innovation and competitive pricing for Indian consumers in a market where health cover is expanding quickly but coverage gaps remain wide.

title: Bank of Canada Holds Rate at 2.25% for Sixth Straight Decision
summary: The Bank of Canada kept its policy rate at 2.25% for a sixth consecutive meeting, signalling growing comfort with holding steady as growth rebounds and it looks through the energy-driven spike in inflation.
description: The Bank of Canada held its target for the overnight rate at 2.25% for a sixth consecutive decision, keeping the bank rate at 2.5% and the deposit rate at 2.20% as policymakers signalled increasing comfort with steady policy. The central bank said Canada's economy is showing signs of improvement, with growth picking up and its sources broadening, even as risks from the Middle East conflict and US trade policy persist. Its accompanying Monetary Policy Report lifted headline inflation projections for 2026, driven by elevated gasoline refinery margins expected to normalise as oil prices ease, while core inflation was still seen hovering around 2% through 2028. Notably, the bank dropped earlier explicit references to the potential need to cut rates if the US imposed new tariffs, or to raise rates if higher oil prices fed generalised inflation, a signal of greater confidence in the current stance. Growth is estimated to have rebounded to about 2.5% in the second quarter after a weak start to the year, with unemployment holding around 6.5%. Governor Tiff Macklem cautioned that the longer energy prices stay elevated, the greater the risk they spill into other goods and services.
image_alt: City financial district representing central bank policy (illustrative)
key_points: The Bank of Canada held its overnight rate at 2.25% for a sixth straight meeting.
It raised 2026 headline inflation projections while keeping core inflation near 2%.
Second-quarter growth is estimated to have rebounded to about 2.5%.
The bank dropped explicit references to potential rate cuts or hikes, signalling comfort with holding.
why_it_matters: A prolonged rate hold keeps borrowing costs steady for Canadian mortgage holders and businesses, offering predictability amid trade and energy uncertainty.

title: Singapore's MAS and Bank of Thailand Sign Cybersecurity and Fraud Pact
summary: The Monetary Authority of Singapore and the Bank of Thailand signed a memorandum of understanding to deepen cooperation on cybersecurity and digital fraud protection, strengthening cross-border defences as scams and cyber threats rise.
description: The Monetary Authority of Singapore and the Bank of Thailand signed a memorandum of understanding to expand cooperation on cybersecurity and digital fraud protection, the Singapore central bank announced. The agreement is designed to strengthen the two authorities' collective ability to counter increasingly sophisticated cyber threats and cross-border scams that target consumers and financial institutions across the region. Under the pact, the regulators are expected to share information, coordinate on incident response and collaborate on measures to protect users of digital financial services, an area of growing concern as payments and banking rapidly move online. The move reflects a broader regional push, including recent central-bank gatherings, to build joint defences against fraud syndicates that operate across borders and exploit gaps between national systems. It also complements Singapore's wider supervisory focus on technology risk and operational resilience, and its public scam-awareness efforts urging consumers to verify unexpected requests to transfer money or share banking credentials. For the financial sector, closer cross-border coordination can speed the detection and disruption of fraud networks, though officials stress that consumer vigilance remains essential, given how quickly scam tactics evolve across messaging platforms and payment channels.
image_alt: Digital security lock representing cybersecurity cooperation in finance (illustrative)
key_points: MAS and the Bank of Thailand signed an MOU on cybersecurity and digital fraud protection.
The pact covers information sharing and coordinated defences against cross-border scams.
It complements Singapore's focus on technology risk and operational resilience.
Officials stress consumer vigilance remains essential as scam tactics evolve.
why_it_matters: Cross-border cooperation helps disrupt fraud syndicates that exploit gaps between national systems, offering better protection for consumers using digital payments and banking.

title: Singapore Central Bank Expected to Hold Policy Steady on July 27
summary: Most economists expect the Monetary Authority of Singapore to leave its exchange-rate-based policy unchanged at its July 27 review, with core inflation still running below the top of the official forecast range.
description: Singapore's central bank is widely expected to keep monetary policy settings unchanged at its scheduled review on July 27, according to a Reuters poll of economists, with inflation seen as manageable even as the Middle East conflict keeps energy costs elevated. Twelve of 16 analysts surveyed expect the Monetary Authority of Singapore to hold, while four anticipate further tightening. Unlike most central banks, the MAS conducts policy through the Singapore dollar's nominal effective exchange rate, known as the S$NEER, adjusting the band's slope, width and midpoint rather than setting an interest rate. The central bank tightened policy in April after leaving settings unchanged at its three previous meetings. Economists point to June core and headline inflation of about 1.6% and 1.9% respectively, both within the official 1.5% to 2.5% forecast range for 2026, as evidence that current settings remain appropriate. Authorities are also watching potential El Nino-related weather disruptions and their possible impact on food prices. The split view matters for the currency: a hold would be consistent with current market pricing, while a surprise tightening could steepen the S$NEER slope and lend support to the Singapore dollar.
image_alt: Singapore skyline representing monetary policy and markets (illustrative)
key_points: 12 of 16 economists expect the MAS to hold policy steady on July 27.
The MAS manages policy via the Singapore dollar's exchange rate, not interest rates.
June core and headline inflation were about 1.6% and 1.9%, within the official range.
A surprise tightening could steepen the S$NEER slope and support the currency.
why_it_matters: The MAS decision influences the Singapore dollar and import costs, affecting inflation and purchasing power in a highly trade-dependent economy.

title: Australia's APRA Proposes Lower Capital Charges for Infrastructure Lending
summary: Australia's banking regulator has opened consultation on changes to bank credit-risk capital rules, including lower risk weights for certain infrastructure, corporate and residential development lending, aiming to support growth while preserving stability.
description: The Australian Prudential Regulation Authority has begun consulting on proposed changes to banks' credit-risk capital settings, including lower risk weights for selected infrastructure, corporate and residential development lending. Under the proposals, large domestic public infrastructure exposures would attract a reduced risk weight, and certain unrated corporate and residential development loans would also see adjustments, effectively lowering the amount of capital banks must hold against these exposures. The regulator frames the changes as a way to support economic growth and competition without compromising the safety and soundness of the financial system, reflecting a broader effort to fine-tune prudential settings so they strike a balance between stability, efficiency and competition. The consultation is part of a busy reform agenda for Australia's regulators, which recently saw the operational-risk standard CPS 230 take full effect and proposed updates to governance requirements across banking, superannuation and insurance. Lower capital charges on infrastructure lending could make it more attractive for banks to finance long-term public projects such as transport, energy and utilities, potentially channelling more private capital into nation-building investment. Industry participants are expected to weigh in on the calibration and scope before the rules are finalised.
image_alt: Bank building representing prudential capital rules (illustrative)
key_points: APRA is consulting on changes to bank credit-risk capital settings.
Proposals include lower risk weights for large domestic public infrastructure lending.
Adjustments would also apply to certain corporate and residential development loans.
The changes aim to support growth and competition while preserving stability.
why_it_matters: Lower capital charges could encourage banks to finance more infrastructure and development, supporting long-term projects while regulators guard financial stability.

title: US Weighs Fed Decision as Cooling Job Market Clouds Rate Path
summary: Investors head into the Federal Reserve's late-July meeting weighing signs of a cooling US labour market against sticky inflation, with second-quarter GDP and the Fed's preferred price gauge due right after the decision.
description: The US Federal Reserve's policy meeting concluding this week arrives against a backdrop of a labour market that is losing momentum, complicating the path for interest rates. Recent hiring data have come in soft, and short-term Treasury yields have eased as investors judged that weaker employment could keep the central bank on hold rather than pushing it toward another hike. Officials have signalled the job market remains broadly healthy but warrants close watching, while flagging persistent pressure on the inflation side of their mandate, partly from tariffs expected to feed through to consumer prices later in the year. The meeting is bracketed by consequential data: second-quarter gross domestic product and the personal consumption expenditures price index, the Fed's preferred inflation measure, are due the day after the decision, giving policymakers and markets a fresh read on whether growth and price pressures are moderating. With energy costs volatile and trade policy uncertain, the Fed faces what several officials describe as a tricky moment for calibrating policy. Markets broadly expect no change at this meeting, keeping attention on the guidance and on how the data shape expectations for the months ahead.
image_alt: Federal Reserve building representing US monetary policy (illustrative)
key_points: The Fed's policy meeting concludes this week amid signs of a cooling labour market.
Soft hiring data pushed short-term Treasury yields lower on reduced hike expectations.
Second-quarter GDP and the PCE inflation gauge are due right after the decision.
Officials flag persistent inflation pressure, partly from tariffs, as a complicating factor.
why_it_matters: The Fed's stance and incoming data drive borrowing costs on mortgages, credit and business loans, and shape the outlook for jobs and inflation across the US economy.

title: UK Regulators Begin Overseeing Critical Technology Providers to Finance
summary: UK financial regulators have started overseeing the first designated Critical Third Parties, extending resilience supervision to major technology and cloud providers whose services underpin banks, insurers and markets.
description: The Bank of England, the Prudential Regulation Authority and the Financial Conduct Authority have begun overseeing the first Critical Third Parties under a new regime that took effect in mid-July, following designation by HM Treasury. Critical Third Parties are technology and other service providers, such as major cloud and infrastructure firms, whose services underpin the smooth functioning of the UK financial system. The regime is designed to strengthen the resilience of these essential providers, recognising that a severe outage or cyber incident at a widely used supplier could ripple across many banks, insurers and market participants at once. Importantly, designation is not the same as authorisation, and oversight is limited to the resilience of the services the providers deliver to UK financial firms rather than their broader business. HM Treasury decides which suppliers fall within scope, generally based on recommendations from the regulators, and the roster is expected to evolve as further designations are considered. The move comes as authorities intensify their focus on operational and cyber resilience, with cyberattacks recently ranked among the top systemic risks by financial firms. Regulators say they will continue working closely with industry and designated providers while supporting innovation and competitiveness.
image_alt: Data centre servers representing critical technology providers to finance (illustrative)
key_points: UK regulators began overseeing the first Critical Third Parties in mid-July 2026.
The regime covers technology and service providers underpinning the financial system.
Oversight is limited to service resilience, not full authorisation of the providers.
HM Treasury decides scope, which will evolve with further designations.
why_it_matters: Concentration among a few big technology suppliers means one failure could hit many financial firms, so overseeing their resilience helps protect everyday banking and insurance services.

title: IRDAI Proposes Reinsurance Order-of-Preference Reform in India
summary: India's insurance regulator has proposed revising the order of preference for placing reinsurance business, a change that could reshape state-owned GIC Re's right of first refusal and open the market to more competition.
description: The Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India has proposed changes to the rules governing the order of preference under which insurers place their reinsurance business, a move that could alter the longstanding advantage held by state-owned General Insurance Corporation of India. A new exposure draft sets out amendments under consideration that would affect GIC Re's right of first refusal, the arrangement that currently gives the national reinsurer priority access to business ceded by Indian insurers. Industry bodies have welcomed the direction, saying the proposals point toward a more open and balanced reinsurance market. Reinsurance allows primary insurers to transfer part of their risk to other companies, strengthening their capacity to underwrite large or catastrophic exposures, and a more competitive placement framework could give insurers greater choice of partners and pricing. The regulator has separately retained the mandatory obligatory cession, the share of business non-life insurers must place with GIC Re, at 4% for the financial year, and continues to identify GIC Re, Life Insurance Corporation and New India Assurance as domestic systemically important insurers. The consultation reflects a broader effort to modernise India's reinsurance sector and align it with the regulator's goal of deeper, more resilient insurance markets.
image_alt: Regulatory documents representing reinsurance rule reform (illustrative)
key_points: IRDAI proposed revising the order of preference for placing reinsurance business.
The change could alter state-owned GIC Re's right of first refusal.
Industry bodies said the reform points to a more open, balanced reinsurance market.
The obligatory cession to GIC Re was retained at 4% for the financial year.
why_it_matters: A more competitive reinsurance framework can improve insurers' choice and pricing, strengthening their capacity to cover large risks and ultimately benefiting policyholders.

title: ECB Unveils Shortlist of New Euro Banknote Designs for Public Vote
summary: The European Central Bank revealed ten shortlisted designs for future euro banknotes across two themes and opened a public survey until September, as it works toward more secure cash with a final design expected by year-end.
description: The European Central Bank unveiled a shortlist of ten designs for future euro banknotes and opened a public consultation, part of a long-running effort to refresh the currency and roll out more secure cash. The candidate designs are grouped under two themes, 'European culture' and 'Rivers and birds', and will now be put to public debate, with Europeans invited to share feedback through a survey open until 21 September. President Christine Lagarde said the central bank expects to select a winning design by the end of the year. The redesign is aimed at strengthening the security features of physical euro notes to stay ahead of counterfeiting, while also modernising imagery that has remained largely unchanged since the euro's launch. Cash remains widely used across the euro area even as digital payments grow, and the ECB has emphasised its commitment to keeping banknotes available and trusted. The exercise runs alongside the central bank's parallel work on a potential digital euro, which officials have stressed would complement rather than replace physical cash. Once a design is chosen, production and issuance of the new notes would follow over the subsequent years.
image_alt: Euro banknotes representing new currency designs (illustrative)
key_points: The ECB unveiled ten shortlisted designs for future euro banknotes.
Designs fall under two themes: 'European culture' and 'Rivers and birds'.
A public survey is open until 21 September, with a final design expected by year-end.
The redesign aims to strengthen security features against counterfeiting.
why_it_matters: New banknote designs affect the cash used daily by hundreds of millions across the euro area, with improved security features helping guard against counterfeiting.

title: US Consumer Watchdog in Focus as Tariffs Threaten to Lift Prices
summary: US households face fresh cost pressures as a temporary blanket import tariff nears a scheduled expiry amid legal challenges, leaving businesses and consumers uncertain about how trade policy will feed into prices later in 2026.
description: US consumers and businesses are watching trade policy closely as a temporary 10% blanket import tariff, authorised under an emergency trade provision, nears a scheduled expiry amid significant legal uncertainty. Earlier in the year, a federal trade court ruled that the administration had exceeded its authority in imposing the surcharge, but the decision did not automatically remove tariff exposure for all importers while the matter moves through appeal. As a result, companies are uncertain whether the short-term surcharges will end, be replaced or transition into another policy framework, complicating planning for input costs, supply chains and pricing. Federal Reserve officials have flagged tariffs as a key reason inflation could tick higher later in the year, expecting the added costs to gradually pass through to consumer prices. For households already navigating elevated energy costs tied to the Middle East conflict, the outcome carries direct implications for the price of imported goods, from electronics to household staples. Analysts note that any change to the tariff regime could materially affect corporate margin expectations and the broader inflation trajectory, making the resolution of the legal and policy questions an important factor for the cost of living and the Fed's rate decisions in the months ahead.
image_alt: Shopping cart with goods representing consumer prices and tariffs (illustrative)
key_points: A temporary 10% blanket import tariff nears a scheduled expiry amid legal uncertainty.
A federal trade court ruled the administration exceeded its authority on the surcharge.
Businesses are unsure whether the tariffs will end, be replaced or change form.
Fed officials expect tariff costs to gradually pass through to consumer prices.
why_it_matters: Tariff decisions directly affect the price of imported goods and the inflation outlook, shaping household budgets and the Federal Reserve's interest-rate path.

title: Australia's RBA Warns Home Insurance Affordability Threatens Mortgage Quality
summary: The Reserve Bank of Australia has flagged that worsening home insurance affordability could raise underinsurance and, over time, erode the credit quality of mortgages, with a regulator's climate assessment due to quantify the risk.
description: The Reserve Bank of Australia has warned that deteriorating home insurance affordability poses a growing challenge with potential systemic implications for the financial system. In its assessment of financial-system resilience, the central bank cautioned that further declines in the affordability of insurance could push more households into underinsurance, which in turn could lower the credit quality of existing mortgage loans, since inadequately insured properties are more exposed to damage that undermines their value and borrowers' finances. Rising premiums have been driven by more frequent and severe natural disasters, higher rebuilding and reinsurance costs, and the growing exposure of homes in high-risk areas to floods, storms and bushfires. The Australian Prudential Regulation Authority's Climate Vulnerability Assessment is expected to help quantify how general insurance affordability may be affected by climate change over the medium term, with results due to be released around the middle of 2026. The issue sits at the intersection of insurance, housing and financial stability, and highlights how climate-related risks can ripple from insurance markets into the banking system. Policymakers and insurers continue to grapple with balancing affordability, risk-based pricing and the need to keep cover accessible for households in exposed regions.
image_alt: Home damaged by storm representing insurance affordability risk (illustrative)
key_points: The RBA warned worsening home insurance affordability could have systemic implications.
Rising underinsurance could lower the credit quality of existing mortgage loans.
Premiums have climbed with more frequent disasters and higher rebuilding costs.
APRA's Climate Vulnerability Assessment is due to quantify the risk around mid-2026.
why_it_matters: As insurance costs climb, more homeowners risk being underinsured, a problem that can spill from insurance markets into housing and the banking system.
